meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas. doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.mechanism: Sustained protein synthesis is what physically builds muscle; in mice, Akt/mTOR signalling is necessary and sufficient for hypertrophy (BOD2001). In people, blocking mTOR blunts the short-term rise in muscle protein synthesis after exercise (DRU2009); whether that changes how much muscle is gained over months was not measured.
data.mechanism_beginner: Ongoing protein-building is what physically builds muscle; in mice, the signals that drive it are needed for muscle growth and are enough to cause it. In people, blocking mTOR blunts the rise in muscle protein-building after a single bout of exercise, but how much muscle is gained over months under the drug was not measured.
data.context: Requires mechanical load. mTORC1 activation without loading does not reproduce healthy hypertrophy, and constitutive activation alone is not sufficient.
data.boundary: Mouse (BOD2001) and cultured myotubes (ROM2001). The human study DRU2009 is cited on the step before this one (LOAD-MTORC1): rapamycin blocked the rise in muscle protein synthesis 1-2 h after one bout of contractions (and also blocked ERK1/2). It did not measure muscle growth, so it is not evidence for this arrow.
data.note: 2026-10-10: DRU2009 moved off this arrow. It measured short-term protein synthesis, not muscle growth, and stays cited on LOAD-MTORC1. Human relevance plausible.
